passage:
The village youth club had a plan: paint the bus shelter blue for the fair. Rajni, the group's leader, had already ordered the paint. Neelam sat cross-legged on the floor, chewing the corner of her dupatta. She knew the rain would wash ordinary paint off within a week; her uncle had told her so about the tank wall. But Rajni was her friend, and everyone else was nodding. Neelam felt hot, torn between loyalty and honesty.

“Rajni,” she finally said, “can I say something? I think the paint will wash away. Maybe the weatherproof kind?” The room went quiet. Rajni frowned, then asked, “How much more is it?” “I can find out from the shop tomorrow,” said Neelam. Rajni nodded slowly. “Okay. Find out.”

qa.q: What had Rajni already ordered?
qa.a: Rajni had already ordered the paint.

qa.q: Why did Neelam feel hot, torn between loyalty and honesty?
qa.a: Neelam valued Rajni's friendship and did not want to break the nodding, yet believed the paint would wash away.

qa.q: What small step did Neelam offer after speaking up?
qa.a: Neelam offered to find out the price of the weatherproof paint from the shop the next day.

qa.q: What might Rajni have felt when Neelam spoke up in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rajni may have felt surprised and briefly defensive, having already ordered the paint, but was willing to listen.

grounding: A teenager in a group disagrees with a decision, feels torn between loyalty and speaking up, and offers an honest contribution.

passage:
The student council at a Birmingham school was planning a fundraiser. Kwame, the president, said, “Bake sale on Friday, done.” Everyone nodded. Selin's stomach twisted. Half the year group would be at mock exams on Friday. She had said yes to the last three ideas because Kwame was a friend and worked hard. Her pen tapped the table. Silent agreement was easier, she thought, but it wouldn't help him.

“Kwame,” she said, “I like the bake sale, but Friday is mock exam day. Could we do Thursday?” Two people looked up with relief. Kwame paused, then grinned a little awkwardly. “Okay. I hadn't checked. Thursday.”

qa.q: What did Kwame propose?
qa.a: Kwame said, “Bake sale on Friday, done.”

qa.q: Why did Selin not speak up on the last three ideas?
qa.a: Selin valued Kwame as a friend and saw how hard Kwame worked, so agreeing felt easier and kinder.

qa.q: What choice did Selin make when Kwame announced Friday?
qa.a: Selin said she liked the bake sale but pointed out the mock exam clash and suggested Thursday.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when Selin questioned Friday?
qa.a: Kwame probably felt a little embarrassed at not checking, but relieved that the problem was found before the event.

grounding: A teenager in a group disagrees with a decision, feels torn between loyalty and speaking up, and gives honest input.

passage:
I'm Suraj, and in Class 9 I learned something about being in someone else's team.
Reena was our group leader for the science exhibition. She's my friend, and she's really smart. She chose the topic: volcanoes. I thought volcanoes were what every group does. I wanted to do rainwater harvesting, because our colony floods every year.
For a week I said nothing. She's my friend, I thought. Don't make it awkward. But I felt grumpy every meeting.
Finally, I said it, quietly, after class. “Reena, can I suggest something? I think we'd stand out with rainwater.”
She thought about it. “Show me tomorrow.” I did. We didn't switch completely, but she added a rainwater model to our table.

qa.q: What topic did Reena choose?
qa.a: She chose volcanoes.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel during the week of saying nothing?
qa.a: Suraj felt torn and grumpy, loyal to Reena but frustrated at not being heard.

qa.q: What made Suraj's way of speaking up effective?
qa.a: Suraj spoke privately, framed it as a suggestion, and brought evidence the next day, which let Reena include the idea.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when Suraj spoke up?
qa.a: She may have been surprised but open, since she asked to see Suraj's idea and added it to the table.

grounding: A teenager recalls being torn between loyalty to a friend's leadership and speaking up, and finding an honest way to contribute.

passage:
Class 11 teacher's note, group project on local history.
Lalremsiami leads Pankaj's group. She is confident and organised, and the group mostly follows her. Today I noticed Pankaj frowning at the plan. He wrote something in his notebook, crossed it out, and said nothing.
After class, he stayed back. “Ma'am, I think we're doing only the famous buildings. Nobody's interviewing old people in the market. But I don't want to go against Siami. She's my friend.”
I told him honest ideas are part of being a good team member, not disloyalty, and suggested he raise it at the next meeting as a question.
He did, today. Lalremsiami said, “Oh, that's good. Pankaj, you lead the interviews.”

qa.q: What did Pankaj think the group was missing?
qa.a: Interviewing old people in the market.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel before talking to the teacher?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty to his friend and wanting to speak up, frowning and crossing out his note.

qa.q: What did the teacher's advice help Pankaj do?
qa.a: It helped him see honest ideas as part of good teamwork and raise it as a question, which Lalremsiami welcomed.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when Pankaj raised his idea?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and open, quickly giving him the interviews to lead.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager torn between loyalty to a friend's leadership and speaking up, and learning honest contribution is good followership.

passage:
Tuesday
Debate practice again. Kalyani is our captain, and she's brilliant. But she wants to start with the weakest argument and save the strongest for last. I think it's the wrong way round. The judges will be bored by then.
I didn't say anything today. Everyone else nodded. She's worked so hard on the order, and I don't want to seem like I'm trying to take over.
But I keep thinking about it. If we lose because of the order, and I knew, that's kind of on me too.
Tomorrow I'll ask her, just us two: “Can we try it the other way once and see?” If she still wants hers, fine. At least I'll have said it.
Arnab

qa.q: What does Kalyani want to save for last?
qa.a: The strongest argument.

qa.q: How is Arnab feeling about the argument order?
qa.a: Arnab feels torn and uneasy, not wanting to seem like taking over, but worried about staying silent.

qa.q: Is Arnab's plan for tomorrow a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; asking privately to try the other order once is honest and respectful, leaving the decision with the captain.

qa.q: How might Kalyani react to the private suggestion?
qa.a: She may be open to trying it, since it's framed as a test rather than a challenge.

grounding: A teenager writes about disagreeing with a captain's plan and feeling torn between loyalty and speaking up, then deciding to contribute honestly.

passage:
Sonali: can I rant for a sec
Noor: go
Sonali: Tanvi decided the whole annual day dance today. which is fine, she's the lead
Sonali: but she put Ishita at the back again. Ishita's literally our best dancer
Noor: did you say anything?
Sonali: no 😬 everyone just nodded. Tanvi's been so nice to me all year. I don't want to seem against her
Noor: saying one thing isn't being against her though
Sonali: I know. but if I say it and nobody backs me I'll look stupid
Noor: what if you tell her privately? like "love the plan, one idea"
Sonali: hmm. ok. typing to her now
Sonali to Tanvi: Loved today's plan!! one thought, what if Ishita does the solo in the middle? she nails those turns
Tanvi: omg you're right. why didn't anyone say this 😅

qa.q: Where did Tanvi put Ishita in the dance?
qa.a: At the back again.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stay quiet at practice?
qa.a: Sonali felt torn and nervous: loyal to Tanvi, who had been kind, and afraid of looking stupid if nobody backed her.

qa.q: Why did Noor's suggested wording work?
qa.a: Starting with genuine support and offering "one idea" privately let Tanvi hear the point without feeling challenged.

qa.q: How does Tanvi seem to take Sonali's idea?
qa.a: Tanvi seems pleased and a little embarrassed that nobody had said it earlier.

grounding: Shows a teenager torn between loyalty to a group leader and speaking up, who finally contributes an honest idea instead of silent agreement.
